workflows.name: Manual control: Unpause, GetPauseState, DenyPacket

trigger.detail: A direct gRPC call to bridgingauthorizer.v1.BridgingAuthorizer on the internal control port. None of these three RPCs has any caller in this monorepo — they are driven by hand, or by tooling that lives in anchorstablecoins/issuance-systems.

workflows.summary: The other three control RPCs. Unpause is how bridging resumes after a kill-switch pull, GetPauseState is how you find out whether it is stopped and why, and DenyPacket permanently blackballs a single LayerZero packet. All three preserve the control-surface principle: none of them can make the authorizer sign something it would otherwise refuse.

steps.title: Unpause lifts the pause — and nothing in this monorepo calls it
steps.detail: Unpause{} clears the pause if there is one and is a no-op when not paused. Two things are worth knowing before you rely on it. First, there is no caller anywhere in this monorepo: Botón can stop bridging but has no code path that restarts it, so resuming is a deliberate human act. Second, Unpause is a plain v1 handler — hardening which identities may call it is tracked separately as STA-1231 and is explicitly NOT enforced by the proto. Combined with the plaintext control port, that means the ability to resume bridging is, as far as this repo can show, no better protected than the ability to halt it. See gap-ba-unpause-unhardened and gap-ba-plaintext-control-plane.

branches.then: the pause is lifted and signing resumes
no-op

steps.title: GetPauseState answers 'is bridging stopped, and why'
steps.detail: Returns four fields: paused (bool), reason (string — for an auto-pause this is the Botón bridge-event alert title), actor (string, who or what paused it), and paused_at_unix (int64, 0 when paused is false). This is the first thing to call when bridge attestations appear to have stopped. It has no caller in this monorepo either, so in practice it is invoked ad hoc against the in-cluster gRPC port.

steps.title: DenyPacket refuses one packet forever
steps.detail: DenyPacket{guid, reason} takes the LayerZero packet GUID as exactly 32 bytes and makes the authorizer refuse to ever sign that packet. It is permanent in v1: there is deliberately no 'allow' counterpart, so a denial cannot be reversed through the API. That irreversibility is the same design principle as the rest of the surface — every control RPC can only subtract from what the authorizer will sign. It is also the narrow-scope alternative to Pause: one packet instead of all bridging. Where denials are stored, and therefore whether they survive a restart, is unconfirmed; see gap-ba-internals-unconfirmed.

steps.title: Who is allowed to call any of this is unconfirmed
steps.detail: The control service is served only on the gRPC port and never through the external HTTPS gateway, which is a real boundary — the public edge cannot reach these RPCs at all. Inside the mesh, though, no authorization mechanism is visible from this repo: the one known client dials with TLS explicitly disabled, and there is no AuthorizationPolicy, no principal allowlist and no token check in the monorepo for this service. Any in-cluster workload that can reach bridgingauthorizer.stablecoins:9091 may be able to pause, unpause or deny. UNCONFIRMED — the server side may well enforce something. See gap-ba-plaintext-control-plane and gap-ba-internals-unconfirmed.

outcomes.meaning: The pause is cleared and the DVN signs again.
outcomes.rollback: Packets the authorizer declined to attest while paused are not retroactively attested by unpausing; LayerZero-side retry behaviour for those packets is outside this repo.

outcomes.meaning: One specific packet GUID will never be attested by this DVN.
outcomes.rollback: None — permanent in v1, with no 'allow' counterpart in the API.

failureHandling: No monorepo caller means no retry policy, no alerting and no audit trail on this side for any of the three RPCs. Whatever the external repo does around them is unconfirmed.
versionMarkers: Unpause identity hardening is deferred to STA-1231.
DenyPacket permanence and the absence of an allow counterpart are explicit v1 choices.

workflows.name: DVN signing (implemented outside this repo)

trigger.detail: A LayerZero packet needing DVN attestation, reaching the sign-only REST API on the public HTTPS edge (bridgingauthorizer.anchorage.com and its per-environment equivalents).

workflows.summary: The authorizer's actual job — attesting LayerZero packets as a DVN — is implemented in anchorstablecoins/issuance-systems and cannot be read from this monorepo. This entry records the little that IS knowable from here, and is deliberately thin. Treat every mechanism below as unconfirmed; see gap-ba-internals-unconfirmed.

steps.title: A packet arrives for attestation at the public sign-only edge
steps.detail: The public HTTPS edge — reserved static IP, Cloud Armor, SSL policy and a Google-managed certificate, all owned by the stablecoins infra-critical stack in the anchorsc-is-<env> project — fronts a REST API that is sign-only. This monorepo publishes only the DNS: bridgingauthorizer.anchorage.com (35.201.115.125), bridgingauthorizer.anchorage-staging.com (34.117.86.118), bridgingauthorizer.anchorage-development.com (34.149.167.237), plus the _acme-challenge CNAMEs for certificate validation. The request shape, authentication and rate limiting of that REST API are UNCONFIRMED — none of it is in this repo. What is confirmed is the negative: the Pause/Unpause/GetPauseState/DenyPacket control service is never exposed here. See gap-ba-internals-unconfirmed.

steps.title: Pre-sign checks: pause state, packet denials, and the authorizer's own rate limit
steps.detail: Three gates are known to exist, though their implementation is not visible here. A global pause blocks all signing (ba-auto-pause). A DenyPacket entry permanently blocks one GUID (ba-manual-control). And the authorizer runs its OWN pre-sign rate-limit check, independent of the OFT adapter's on-chain rate-limit configuration — Botón's response matrix relies on exactly that independence, noting that a tampered on-chain rate-limit config alone does not bypass the cap because the authorizer still enforces its own. The limits, their scope and their storage are all UNCONFIRMED. See gap-ba-internals-unconfirmed.

branches.when: paused, or the packet GUID was denied, or the rate limit is exceeded
branches.then: no attestation is produced
the authorizer signs

steps.title: Signing under the DVN identity, then attesting on chain
steps.detail: The on-chain identity is the per-chain dvnSignerAddress from lzconfig — a secp256k1 signer identity for the DVN committee rather than an on-chain account, which is why it stays hex-encoded regardless of the chain's VM. lzconfig enforces that a chain with a dvnSignerAddress also carries a vid (verifier id) greater than zero, since the signer commits to that verifier id and the two only make sense together. These trust anchors, along with the EndpointV2, SendUln302, ReceiveUln302, OFTAdapter, ProxyAdmin and DVN contract addresses, are embedded per environment in the binary and immutable at runtime — no mounted file, env var or dynamic refresh to tamper with — and are shared with mintburn and Botón. Where the private key behind dvnSignerAddress actually lives is UNCONFIRMED: Cloud KMS is the plausible home given the rest of the platform, but no key ring, key name or IAM binding for it appears anywhere in this monorepo. The chain RPC endpoints the authorizer reads to verify a packet before attesting are likewise unconfirmed. See gap-ba-internals-unconfirmed.

outcomes.meaning: The DVN signature exists and the destination chain can verify the packet. Mechanism unconfirmed.
outcomes.rollback: An attestation cannot be withdrawn. DenyPacket only prevents future signing of a GUID; it does not revoke a signature already issued.

failureHandling: Unconfirmed. Retry, backoff and dead-letter behaviour for the signing path are all in the external repo. The only failure signal reaching this monorepo's tooling is error-level logs in Datadog, which the 'bridgingauthorizer error log rate' monitor watches.

journeys.title: Customer mint, endorsed by autopen
journeys.summary: A customer converts fiat into an Anchorage-issued stablecoin from the client dashboard. mintburn takes the request through a customer quorum gate, moves the underlying asset, creates the on-chain mint operation, and stablecoins-autopen endorses it with an attested certificate instead of a second human quorum. Botón later reconciles the on-chain mint against internal records.

steps.text: An org user submits a conversion in the client dashboard convert modal, which calls mintburn through federated GraphQL (createMintBurnConversion) or REST v2 POST /stablecoins/conversion.

IssueRedeemConversionRequestHandler holds the customer funds, creates an off-chain VISUAL_APPROVAL signing operation targeted at its child workflow, starts that child, and returns the IssueRedeem ID plus the authorization operation ID.

IssueRedeemConversionRequestExecution waits on the OFFCHAIN_VISUAL_APPROVAL_SIGNING_RESULT signal (the customer quorum gate), checks the signing outcome, passes the issuer-review step, then dispatches the ISSUE child workflow.
IssueOperation sets the record to EXECUTING, transfers the underlying fiat holdings, releases holds, and creates the generic execute operation whose signer is the asset config MinterBurnerRole.

mintburn polls custody until the operation reaches SIGS_REQUIRED, then calls EndorseExecuteOperation over mTLS to the CVM; the gateway runs its ordered policy chain, reserves an audit row, and signs a CertEndorsementPayload with its attested Ed25519 identity.

custody submits the certificate endorsement and the HSM re-enforces the same rules at sign time (organization allowlist, decision must be APPROVE, endorsedParamsDigest must bind to the endorsed parameters), so the two allowlists must stay in sync.

The mint transaction is broadcast and confirmed on chain; mintburn is woken by the ON_CHAIN_CONFIRMATION signal, polls the operation to a final state, and independently re-reads the chain via rpc-lib before declaring EXECUTED.
Hexagate's monitor on the token contract observes the mint and posts a signed webhook to Botón at /webhooks/hexagate/primary-market-issuance.

MintBurnValidation looks up the custody operation by transaction hash with long backoff, matches it to a mintburn IssueRedeem record, compares operation type, counterparty address and amount, and pages incident.io only on a discrepancy.

journeys.title: Coinductor automated mint and withdrawal
journeys.summary: A customer fiat deposit triggers an endorsed automation policy: mintburn mints without any per-operation human action, then tries to push the minted tokens out through an automated withdrawal. The withdrawal leg is built but denied in production today, so the automation run usually stops short of COMPLETED.

steps.text: custody publishes a FiatDepositCompletedEvent (or a DepositAttributionHoldChangeEvent for the burn direction) that mintburn's Pub/Sub subscriber receives as the automation trigger.

The trigger handler applies the soft-fail validation gates - positive amount, matching policy type, organization and vault, source org not the issuer for MINT - and acknowledges and skips the message when any gate fails.

dispatchAutomationRun writes an automation run row and a conversion record, then starts the deterministic {issueRedeemID}-coinductor-automation workflow; an AlreadyStarted error is swallowed so redelivery is safe.
The automation holds the customer funds and runs IssueOperation as a child workflow, which performs the fiat move and creates the on-chain mint operation exactly as in the customer-initiated path.

stablecoins-autopen endorses the mint; the coinductor-run augmentation and cross-check policies confirm that a matching automation run exists and that its status, organization, amount and asset agree with the operation.
With the mint EXECUTED, MaybeCreateAutomatedWithdrawal creates a custody withdraw operation carrying an AutopenInitiator_V1, made idempotent by the run's WithdrawalOperationID.

AutoEndorseAutomatedWithdrawal asks the gateway to endorse the withdrawal. In production ASSET_ALLOWLIST_WITHDRAWAL is empty and MAX_AMOUNT_WITHDRAWAL is 0, so every withdrawal is denied pending STA-1195/1196.
If endorsed, the withdrawal operation still passes through custody risk review and settlement, which can take days; mintburn polls CheckAutomatedWithdrawal with exponential backoff throughout.
finalizeAutomationRun marks the run COMPLETED only once the withdrawal settles; a failed withdrawal yields FAILED with reason AUTOMATED_WITHDRAWAL_FAILED, and the mint is not rolled back.

journeys.title: Suspicious bridge event pauses the DVN
journeys.summary: An administrative or anomalous event on a LayerZero bridging contract is detected by Hexagate, classified by Botón against the Role x Impact response matrix, and - for the highest-impact cases - used to pull the kill switch on bridgingauthorizer so it stops attesting packets.

steps.text: An event fires on an Anchorage-owned LayerZero contract (EndpointV2, SendUln302/ReceiveUln302, an OFT adapter, its ProxyAdmin, or the DVN contract) - for example an admin role change, a nilified packet, or a configuration write.
A Hexagate monitor, configured by hand in the Hexagate UI, matches the event and POSTs a signed webhook to Botón at /webhooks/hexagate/secondary-market-issuance.

Botón caps the body at 16KiB, verifies the RSA-PSS X-Hexagate-Signature, starts SecondaryMarketBridgeEvaluationWorkflow keyed on transaction hash plus event ID, and returns 2xx immediately because Hexagate does not resend on 500.

EvaluateBridgeEvent resolves the contract address and chain through the lzconfig-backed BridgeContractRegistry, parses the event name, and looks the (contract, event) pair up in the classification matrix to get a catalog case, tier, blast radius, shouldPage and shouldPause.

Test-token gating suppresses any pause and downgrades T0 to T1, while paging always fires; unknown contracts, unparseable details and unmapped pairs become non-retryable INVALID_INPUT and show up as drift detectors on the boton.bridge.events counter.

PageBridgeEvent raises an incident.io alert deduped per chain, contract, transaction, event and event ID. Paging is the human backstop, so a page failure fails the workflow while a pause failure does not.

PauseAuthorizer calls Pause with the alert title as the reason, run concurrently with the page. Pause is idempotent and global in v1, and the control surface can only ever make the authorizer stop signing.
With the authorizer paused, its DVN identity stops attesting LayerZero packets, so cross-chain bridging of the affected stablecoins cannot be verified until an operator unpauses.

journeys.title: Monthly stablecoin rewards payout
journeys.summary: Ops staff drive a monthly rewards run from the Payouts Retool app: stablecoinrewards aggregates BigQuery yield data into per-participant payouts, fans out one child workflow per payout, settles each through the Settlement Network, and waits for settlement events to close the payout out.

steps.text: A staff user opens the Payouts Retool app and triggers SavePayouts for a month; an EstimatePayouts variant produces ESTIMATED rows for a dry run instead.
StablecoinRewardsSavePayouts reads the daily yield table from BigQuery and aggregates it into monthly per-participant PENDING payout rows.
Staff review the saved payouts and press Submit Payouts, which calls the payMonthlyStablecoinRewards GraphQL mutation.

StablecoinRewardsMonthlyPayouts loads all PENDING payouts for the date and starts one SinglePayout child per payout with the payout ID as the workflow ID and an ABANDON parent-close policy; the fan-out is unbounded today.

StablecoinRewardsSinglePayout checks the payout is still PENDING, guards against an existing settlement, then calls Settlement Network CreateTwoWaySettlement with clientReferenceId stablecoin-reward-<payoutID>, moves the payout to CREATED, and writes a payout_settlements row.
The Settlement Network executes the two-way settlement between the sender Atlas participant's default vault and the recipient participant's per-network wallet, delegating the on-chain leg to custody.

The default-settlement-events-stablecoinrewards Pub/Sub subscriber maps each SettlementEvent to a payout ID, signals the SinglePayout workflow on SETTLEMENT_EVENTS, and acknowledges; an unknown settlement id is acknowledged and ignored.

SinglePayout consumes settlement signals until a final state and sets the payout to COMPLETED, ACTION_NEEDED, FAILED, REJECTED or TIMED_OUT; a mismatched settlement id is a hard error, and the workflow has no timeout today.

journeys.title: Stablecoin asset config change under quorum
journeys.summary: Changing a stablecoin's asset configuration - including the MinterBurnerRole signer used for every mint and burn - is gated by a visual-approval quorum. mintburn stores the signed endorsements alongside the config and rebuilds the signed payload byte-for-byte when the config is read back.

steps.text: Staff (or an issuer-side caller) invoke RegisterStablecoinConfiguration on mintburn's gRPC API, which records a PENDING asset config change request.
AssetConfigChangeApproval starts with workflow ID {assetTypeID}-asset-config-change-approval and an ALLOW_DUPLICATE reuse policy, so several pending changes to the same asset can be in flight.
CreateAssetConfigApprovalSigning builds the deterministic VisualSignPayload JSON, hashes it with SHA256, and creates a visual-approval signing operation whose signal target is the workflow itself.
The visual-approval operation surfaces to the organization's quorum members for review, showing the human-readable payload rather than raw calldata.
Quorum members sign the visual payload on their devices and the signatures are verified against the HSM-backed key material, producing the endorsements that will be stored with the config.

The workflow awaits ASSET_CONFIG_APPROVAL_SIGNING_RESULT and then runs ResolveAssetConfigApproval, which either persists the new configuration together with its endorsements or marks the request REJECTED.
On approval the workflow signals ChannelDelayCompletion so the caller's request channel is released rather than left hanging on the quorum.

On every later read of the asset config, mintburn rebuilds the VisualSignPayload and byte-compares it against the stored endorsements, so a tampered config fails verification; this re-verification is behind the release-mintburn-verify-asset-config-endorsements flag, which is missing from deploy/ldcli/flags.json.

journeys.title: CVM boot, attestation and certificate rotation
journeys.summary: stablecoins-autopen has no long-lived signing key. Every boot generates an ephemeral identity inside an Intel TDX confidential VM, proves the running measurements to the HSM, and receives a 48-hour certificate chain; the instance deliberately restarts at about 40 hours to rotate.

steps.text: The Ironclave Release Orchestrator builds a reproducible UKI, computes the expected TDX measurements, has them HSM-signed, bakes a GCE image and rolls the managed instance group; Terraform ignores MIG version changes so the image is set out of band.
The init script selects the per-project environment and runs see-runner, which generates an ephemeral Ed25519 key inside the CVM together with a CSR for CN stablecoins-autopen.anchorage.internal.

see-runner takes a nonce over the CSR, collects a TDX quote and the CCEL event log, and fetches a staff token for cvm-address-provider@anchorage.internal so it can reach the HSM risk GraphQL API over IAP.

An "approve boot measurements" operation is raised against HSM_CVM_ORG_KEY_ID; the HSM checks the quote and measurements and returns a signed payload. The CVM polls up to 150 times at 2s, and a failure sleeps 30s and retries rather than serving unattested.

set_credentials turns the HSM-signed payload into a 48-hour leaf certificate chain, which is passed to the /stablecoins-autopen binary on stdin as JSON; there is no PEM fallback, so a failed attestation fails closed.

The process serves gRPC on 8099 behind mTLS with a client OU allowlist of mintburn, plus a plaintext health listener on 8098; once the MIG health check passes, the internal TCP-proxy load balancer routes traffic to the instance.

Every endorsement re-checks the certificate at sign time and refuses with ErrCertNearExpiry when less than 7 hours remain, so an instance that missed its rotation stops endorsing instead of signing with a stale identity.

A jittered SIGTERM at roughly 40 hours (cert_rotation.go) restarts the init loop, re-running see-runner for a fresh attestation and certificate; the 40h + 7h <= 48h invariant is what keeps the two replicas always able to sign.

glossary.definition: mintburn's record of one issue, redeem, bridge or swap conversion, and the entity whose state machine the ISSUE_REDEEM workflows drive. Its states run INITIATED, EXECUTING, AUTHORIZED through terminal EXECUTED, FAILED, REJECTED or TIMED_OUT.

mintburn's automation feature: an endorsed per-organization policy that mints or burns automatically when a fiat deposit or deposit-attribution hold event arrives, with no human action per operation. Policies themselves are quorum-endorsed, and each firing produces an automation run row.

Short name for automated endorsement: the mechanism that lets a machine identity, rather than a human quorum, approve low-risk stablecoin operations. Used loosely for the feature, the service and the delegation model.

The name of the service in the monorepo source tree (source/go/service/autopengateway) that implements automated endorsement. It is the same binary that runs as the stablecoins-autopen CVM, so the two names refer to one system seen from code and from runtime.

The deployed runtime name of autopengateway: two Intel TDX confidential VM replicas per environment, reached only by mintburn over mTLS on port 8099. It endorses generic execute and withdraw operations with an attested Ed25519 identity and an X.509 chain.

Anchorage's confidential-computing platform: dedicated GCP projects (anchorage-ironclave-dev/staging/production), a release orchestrator that builds attestable images, and HSM-backed boot approval. stablecoins-autopen is one of its tenants, alongside hsm-native and cvm-privacy-ristretto.

Confidential VM: a virtual machine whose memory is encrypted and whose boot state can be cryptographically proven to a remote verifier. stablecoins-autopen runs in a CVM in a managed instance group rather than on GKE, which is why it has no Helm-based deploy path.

Intel Trust Domain Extensions, the CPU feature that backs Anchorage's confidential VMs. A TDX quote plus the CCEL event log is what the CVM presents to the HSM to prove which image and measurements it booted.

The in-CVM helper that runs before the service binary: it generates the ephemeral Ed25519 signing key and CSR, takes a TDX quote over a nonce, gets boot measurements approved by the HSM, and hands the resulting 48-hour certificate chain to the service on stdin.

Unified Kernel Image: a single bundled kernel, initrd and command line that can be measured as one artifact. The Ironclave Release Orchestrator builds the UKI reproducibly so its TDX measurements can be pre-computed and HSM-signed before the image ever boots.

An approval attached to a custody operation that lets it proceed to signing. Endorsements normally come from human quorum members; autopen produces a certificate-based endorsement instead, submitted via custody EndorseOperationWithCert and re-validated by the HSM.

An off-chain custody operation that shows a human-readable, deterministic JSON payload for quorum members to review and sign, instead of raw transaction data. mintburn uses it for the customer conversion gate and for asset config changes, hashing the payload with SHA256 and rebuilding it byte-for-byte on verification.

The threshold set of authorized human signers an organization requires to approve an operation. The point of autopen is to satisfy the endorsement requirement for low-risk, repetitive stablecoin operations without assembling a quorum each time.

A signal mintburn sends to release a caller's request channel once a long-running approval has resolved, so the API call does not stay blocked on the quorum. It is sent from the issue/redeem execution, asset config approval and manual deposit workflows.

Decentralized Verifier Network: in LayerZero, an independent party that attests that a cross-chain packet was really emitted on the source chain. Anchorage runs its own DVN through bridgingauthorizer, identified on chain by a per-environment signer address.

The LayerZero Omnichain Fungible Token adapter contract that locks or burns a stablecoin on the source chain and mints it on the destination chain. Adapters are token-scoped in lzconfig and carry the wallets-by-role map for admin, fee, rate-limit and pauser duties.

The chain-wide LayerZero messaging endpoint contract that every OApp on that chain sends through. Botón treats some EndpointV2 events - InboundNonceSkipped, PacketBurnt and clear calls - as unconditional auto-pause cases.

LayerZero's Ultra Light Node message libraries, chain-wide contracts that hold the send and receive verification configuration - including which DVNs and how many confirmations are required. Configuration writes on them classify as security-stack changes in Botón's matrix.

LayerZero endpoint ID: the protocol-level identifier for a chain inside the LayerZero network, distinct from the EVM chain ID. It is stored per chain in lzconfig alongside the vm kind, networkId and chainId.

The verifier ID recorded per chain in lzconfig, used to identify Anchorage's verifier when interacting with LayerZero contracts. Like the other lzconfig fields it is embedded in the binary and immutable at runtime.

The per-environment on-chain address that signs Anchorage's DVN attestations, and therefore the on-chain identity of bridgingauthorizer. It is a trust anchor in lzconfig, so changing it is treated as a security change rather than a config tweak.

The third-party on-chain monitoring vendor that watches Anchorage-owned contracts and posts signed webhooks to Botón. Its monitor set is configured by hand in the Hexagate UI, and it reports some chains with negative IDs (Hoodi -376, Celo -377, Morph -372) that Botón remaps.

The response matrix that maps a (contract role, event) pair to a catalog case, a tier, a blast radius and the decisions to page and to pause. It is the classification table Botón's bridge evaluation encodes in classify.go.

The named anomaly bucket a bridge event is classified into - for example UpgradeAuthorityAnomaly, DVNAttestationAnomaly or RateLimitConfigAnomaly. There are twelve, and the pseudo-cases unmapped, unknown_contract and unparseable act as drift detectors on the boton.bridge.events counter.

How much damage a classified bridge event could cause, ordered Liveness, LivenessOutbound, Malicious, CriticalUnboundedMint. It is one axis of the response matrix and drives whether the verdict includes pausing the authorizer.
The urgency tiers in the response matrix: T0 pages the bridging on-call, T1 pages a broader group. Both page today, and test-token deployments are downgraded from T0 to T1.

The dvnType tier recorded per DVN and adapter contract in lzconfig. Test-token deployments never auto-pause, because pause is global in v1 and a test contract must not be able to freeze production bridging lanes, and their admin wallets are lower assurance.

The client-entities affiliate at the top of an organization's hierarchy. Stablecoin Rewards participants are one-to-one with top-level affiliates, so an organization with no TLA in an allowed jurisdiction cannot see the rewards page.

A participant record in the Settlement Network (internally called Atlas) representing one side of a settlement. Enrolling a top-level affiliate creates or reuses its Atlas participant and adds it as a trusted counterparty of the sender organization.

The Anchorage platform service that moves assets between participants and owns the on-chain leg. stablecoinrewards has no chain RPC dependencies of its own precisely because it delegates asset movement here.

The Settlement Network primitive stablecoinrewards uses to pay a reward: a settlement with both legs defined, created with clientReferenceId stablecoin-reward-<payoutID> and an idempotency key of <payoutID>-<attempt>. Its lifecycle events come back over Pub/Sub and signal the waiting payout workflow.

The shared Go persistence pattern where a row keeps its payload in a single jsonb `data` column instead of typed columns. mintburn's twelve tables use it, which is why schema changes are usually code changes rather than migrations.

Anchorage's internal wrapper library over the Temporal SDK, used by all four Go services here. It supplies the deterministic workflow-ID conventions, the RunChildWorkflow wrapper and the cancellation handling that the workflow termination model relies on.

A Temporal versioning call that lets a workflow change behaviour without breaking replay of runs already in flight; each marker has a stable id such as bounded-tla-fan-out. mintburn carries more than fifteen of them, which makes old code paths permanent until every affected run has closed.

The named Temporal queue a worker polls, which is how one process can host several independent workflow families. mintburn runs five (ISSUE_REDEEM, COINDUCTOR, TOKENIZATION, MANUAL_DEPOSIT, RESERVES_COMPOSITION); Botón runs BOTON and stablecoinrewards runs STABLECOINREWARDS.

Issuance and redemption at the token contract itself - mint against fiat, burn back to fiat. Here autopen is the automated authority and Botón is the watcher, cross-checking Hexagate mint and burn webhooks against custody and mintburn records.

Movement of already-issued tokens between chains over LayerZero bridging. Here bridgingauthorizer is the automated authority as a DVN and Botón is the watcher that classifies events, pages and can pull the pause kill switch.

The autopen policy that denies an endorsement when total minted plus burned value in the trailing 24 hours would exceed ROLLING_WINDOW_CAP_AMOUNT. It is why the CVM needs a database: the endorsement audit log is the window's source of truth, and a crashed PROCESSING row keeps counting, which is deliberately conservative.

The scheduled mintburn workflow that pulls reserve-backing data from BigQuery three times a day (17, 20 and 23 UTC) and stores a snapshot per stablecoin and report date, including total supply on network, total reserves, the reserve ratio and its components. Snapshots carry two verifier fields but pass through no quorum.

The two non-stablecoin asset families mintburn also mints and burns, on the TOKENIZATION queue. Tokenized deposits are auto-endorsed, while tokenized gold sets autoEndorse=false so each operation needs a manual quorum, and only one gold operation per asset may be in flight.

The path for crediting a customer fiat deposit that did not arrive through the normal rails: an off-chain approval operation is created, a quorum endorses it, and mintburn then submits the deposit to bankadapter with a deterministic ID. A known gap is that the off-chain operation is not a child workflow, so the run can get stuck.

The issuer-facing dashboard and its backend-for-frontend, which live outside this monorepo and reach mintburn over REST v2 and gRPC. Issuers are therefore an actor at the edge of the atlas rather than an owned frontend.

The internal low-code tool that hosts the ops surfaces for these systems - the Stablecoin Rewards Onboarding and Payouts apps, swap manual reserve movements, and asset config registration. It reaches services as the retoolv3 Istio principal over gRPC and GraphQL.

The internal debugging surface that staff use to inspect and poke services directly; it is one of the allowed gRPC callers of mintburn. Together with Retool it covers the ops needs that would otherwise require an owned backoffice frontend.

Google Cloud's delivery pipeline service, used for the GKE services here: mintburn, Botón and stablecoinrewards promote dev to staging to prod, with approval gates on staging and prod. stablecoins-autopen does not use it - its images ship through the Ironclave Release Orchestrator instead.

The Terraform automation platform that owns each service's infrastructure stacks. Access posture differs sharply: Botón uses PAM just-in-time access with near-zero standing permissions, while stablecoinrewards has broad standing permissions.

The service-mesh rule that lists which workload identities may call a given port, and the main in-cluster access control for these services. It is how mintburn's gRPC port is limited to graphql-monolith, devdebug, retoolv3, custodystatements and Botón, and how Botón's HTTP port is limited to GCP load-balancer ranges.

Google's Identity-Aware Proxy, used where a caller is outside the mesh. stablecoins-autopen reaches the HSM risk GraphQL API over IAP with a staff token during boot approval, and exports its OTLP telemetry over IAP in development only - which is why its production SLO currently has no data.

gaps.title: mintburn/CLAUDE.md is stale and misleading
gaps.detail: The service's own CLAUDE.md still describes a Paxos integration path and the packages business/mintburn, clients/paxos and app/mintburnworker plus a MINT_BURN Temporal queue. None of those exist. The live service has five queues (ISSUE_REDEEM, COINDUCTOR, TOKENIZATION, MANUAL_DEPOSIT, RESERVES_COMPOSITION). Anyone onboarding from that file will build a wrong mental model. The brief also reports, unconfirmed, that there is no stblcn-dev devstack stack for mintburn, which that doc may also contradict.
gaps.verifyBy: Read source/go/service/mintburn/CLAUDE.md next to the actual package tree and the registered Temporal queues, then rewrite it; ask the stablecoins engineering team who owns the update.

gaps.title: Issuer review appears to be hardcoded to auto-approve
gaps.detail: The brief flags, as unconfirmed, that the issuer-review step in the issue/redeem path is hardcoded to auto-approve rather than waiting on a real issuer decision. If that is true, a control that reads like a human gate in the workflow diagram is not a gate at all, which matters for both risk review and for anyone reasoning about conversion authorization.
gaps.verifyBy: Read the issuer-review activity and the ISSUER_WORKFLOW_REVIEW_RESULT signal handling in source/go/service/mintburn, then confirm intended behaviour with the stablecoins engineering team.

gaps.title: Dead Paxos and fiat-client configuration still shipped in Helm
gaps.detail: ANCHOR_PAXOS_* environment variables are still set in the Helm chart although the Paxos path is gone, and ANCHOR_FIAT_LOCATION is dead too - mintburn has no fiat client and reaches fiat rails only through bankadapter. Dead config invites false assumptions about which integrations are live and shows up as noise in every values file review.
gaps.verifyBy: Grep deploy/services/mintburn for ANCHOR_PAXOS_ and ANCHOR_FIAT_LOCATION, confirm nothing in source/go/service/mintburn reads them, then delete them.

gaps.title: Staging SLO is not managed in Terraform
gaps.detail: slo_mintburn.tf codifies only the production SLO. The staging equivalent is not in Terraform, so it either does not exist or exists only as hand-made Datadog state that nothing protects. STA-1371 tracks codifying it (commit e07448d8) together with aligning the monitor shape to 15-minute windows at 1%.
gaps.verifyBy: Check slo_mintburn.tf for a staging resource and compare with what exists in the Datadog UI; follow STA-1371.

gaps.title: No Datadog dashboard for mintburn in Terraform
gaps.detail: There is no mintburn dashboard defined in Terraform; monitor.tf contains only the Cloud SQL baseline monitors. The Cortex service entity also has its dashboards, alerts, links, on_call, sentry and slack fields null, so an on-call engineer has no codified starting point beyond the single SLO monitor.
gaps.verifyBy: Search the Datadog Terraform directory for a mintburn dashboard resource and check the Datadog UI for a hand-made one; confirm with the stablecoins engineering team whether one exists outside Terraform.

gaps.title: boton is allowlisted from two namespaces and it is unclear which is live
gaps.detail: The Istio allowlist on port 9091 admits boton from both namespace boton and namespace stablecoins. A parallel namespace migration is in flight for autopengateway (flag migration-mintburn-autopengateway-stablecoins-namespace), so the duplicate boton entry is probably migration residue - but which deployment actually calls mintburn today is unconfirmed. Relatedly, the brief reports that bridgingauthorizer is called by boton and not by mintburn, so mintburn holds no bridgingauthorizer client.
gaps.verifyBy: Check which boton Deployment exists per environment and which service account appears in mintburn's 9091 access logs; then trim the allowlist.

gaps.title: Manual-deposit off-chain approval operation is not a child workflow and can stay stuck
gaps.detail: ManualDepositApprovalWorkflow creates the off-chain approval operation with CreateManualDepositOffChainApproval, but that operation is not modelled as a child workflow. Nothing ties its lifetime to the approval workflow's, so if the workflow ends without an approval the operation is not cancelled or cleaned up and can remain open, awaiting a signature that will never be applied. The deposit record itself is safe (the deferred handler marks it REJECTED unless approved), so the impact is an orphaned operator-facing operation rather than a wrong fiat credit; it is confusing to operators and needs manual tidy-up. The research brief records this as a known gap; the exact blast radius and whether any cleanup path exists elsewhere have not been confirmed with the team.
gaps.verifyBy: Read the ManualDepositApprovalWorkflow implementation and CreateManualDepositOffChainApproval in source/go/service/mintburn (MANUAL_DEPOSIT queue) to see whether the off-chain operation has any cancellation or cleanup path; then confirm with engineering-stablecoins-team (#team-stablecoins-eng) whether stuck approval operations have been seen in production.

gaps.title: Unpause has no identity hardening and no known caller
gaps.detail: The proto states plainly that Unpause is a plain v1 handler today and that hardening which identities may call it is tracked separately as STA-1231 and is not enforced by the proto. No caller for Unpause exists anywhere in this monorepo, so resuming bridging after a kill-switch pull is an undocumented manual act. The asymmetry that makes the control surface safe — a caller can only make the authorizer stop signing — protects against a malicious pause, but says nothing about an unauthorized unpause, which would resume attestations while an incident is still open.
gaps.verifyBy: Read STA-1231 for the intended hardening, and check the external repo for any gRPC interceptor or IAM check on Unpause. Ask the team what the documented runbook step for resuming bridging is.

gaps.title: Botón to authorizer is plaintext mesh gRPC and caller authorization is unknown
gaps.detail: The vendored client dials the control port with grpcutil.CreateGRPCConnectionWithoutTLS — plaintext, no mTLS — to bridgingauthorizer.stablecoins:9091. No AuthorizationPolicy, principal allowlist or token check for this service exists in the monorepo, and the proto does not describe one. So from this side, any workload that can reach that address in the cluster may be able to pause, unpause or deny packets. The mitigating facts are that the control service is never exposed through the external HTTPS gateway, and that the surface is subtractive by design, so the worst case through it is halted bridging rather than a fraudulent attestation. Whether the mesh in is-production-gke enforces mTLS or an authorization policy at the infrastructure layer, and whether the server enforces caller identity itself, is unconfirmed.
gaps.verifyBy: Check the is-production-gke mesh configuration and any Istio AuthorizationPolicy for the stablecoins namespace in anchorstablecoins/issuance-systems, plus any gRPC interceptor on the control service. Compare with mintburn's authorizationpolicy.yaml as the monorepo precedent.

gaps.title: The control proto is a hand-synced copy that can silently drift
gaps.detail: source/shared/protobufs/bridgingauthorizer/v1/bridgingauthorizer.proto is a manually synced copy of the source of truth in anchorstablecoins/issuance-systems, taken so that Botón (STA-1230) could generate a typed client without a cross-repo Go module dependency, for which there is no precedent in this repo. The file's own header warns that the package, service and message shapes must stay byte-identical, because gRPC routes on the literal "<package>.<Service>/<Method>" path — so a rename on either side breaks the call at runtime even though the Go types still compile and every test passes. There is no automated check, no CI diff and no version pin enforcing the sync; it depends entirely on whoever edits the external proto remembering this copy exists.
gaps.verifyBy: Diff this file against services/bridgingauthorizer/proto/bridgingauthorizer.proto in anchorstablecoins/issuance-systems, and propose a CI check or a generated-client publishing step so drift fails a build instead of a production pause.

gaps.title: No SLO, and only logs reach Datadog
gaps.detail: bridgingauthorizer has no SLO — slo.name is 'none yet' and its status is unmanaged. The single monitor, 'bridgingauthorizer error log rate', is a log alert firing on any error-level production log in the last hour. The reason is sparsity, and it is a good reason rather than an oversight: production traffic is roughly 46 log events per 24 hours with zero errors observed, so a ratio SLI over 15-minute windows would have an empty denominator most of the time. The consequences are still real: there is no latency or availability objective, no error budget, and the Cortex catalog entity has apm = null and slos = null, so the service shows as unmonitored in the catalog. The monitor's numeric id also has to be hand-wired into cortex-catalog/services_stablecoins.tf after the datadog-monitors stack applies, because the cortex-catalog stack does not read remote_state from datadog-monitors. Unlike every other stablecoins service, bridgingauthorizer is not trace-based: OTLP traces and metrics are wired in issuance-systems PR 153 under STA-1330, but that pipeline is not yet steady-state.
gaps.verifyBy: Track STA-1330 to steady state, then migrate to a formula-based error-rate query paired with an SLO mirroring slo_autopengateway.tf, and hand-wire the monitor id into the Cortex entity.

It looks like copy-paste residue and is misleading to anyone reading the file for the first time; it should be removed or replaced with a real reference.
gaps.verifyBy: read source/go/service/gethwatcher/ethcontracts/stablecoins.go:13-14 and confirm with the Protocols C team that the link is residue before deleting it

gaps.title: lzconfig schema supports SVM but no SVM chain is populated
gaps.detail: Chain.vm accepts EVM or SVM, but every chain in every environment file (production, development, staging, local) is EVM. There is therefore no worked example of what an SVM entry looks like, and the SVM path through the schema is unexercised — the Solana bridging story is not yet represented in lzconfig.
gaps.verifyBy: grep "SVM" across source/go/lib/lzconfig/data/*.json; ask the team whether an SVM bridging pathway is planned

gaps.title: Spacelift stacks and service Terraform for the stablecoins systems have no CODEOWNERS entry
gaps.detail: spacelift/stack_mintburn.tf and stack_stablecoinrewards.tf, and the terraform/services directories for mintburn, stablecoinrewards and autopengateway, are not matched by any CODEOWNERS rule. The same is true of the hand-synced bridgingauthorizerproto and bridgingauthorizer.proto. Infrastructure that controls production deploys and the DVN proto contract can therefore be changed without a stablecoins reviewer.
gaps.verifyBy: read .github/CODEOWNERS and check for patterns matching spacelift/stack_mintburn.tf, spacelift/stack_stablecoinrewards.tf, terraform/services/{mintburn,stablecoinrewards,autopengateway}/ and the bridgingauthorizer proto paths; confirm intended owner with the stablecoins engineering team

gaps.title: Cortex service catalog definitions for the stablecoins systems are unowned
gaps.detail: cortex-catalog/services_stablecoins.tf has no CODEOWNERS entry. The Cortex entities for these five systems are already hand-wired with null dashboards, alerts, links, on-call, Sentry and Slack fields, so nothing prevents further drift between the catalog and reality.
gaps.verifyBy: read .github/CODEOWNERS for a rule covering cortex-catalog/services_stablecoins.tf, and compare that file's entity fields against the live Datadog/Cortex entries

gaps.title: Buildkite pipelines for boton and the banking_solutions stablecoins jobs are unowned
gaps.detail: .buildkite/pipelines/boton/deploy-boton.cue and the banking_solutions deploy- and pre-merge- pipelines for mintburn and stablecoinrewards have no CODEOWNERS entry. CI definitions that gate these deploys can be edited without review from the owning team, and the banking_solutions grouping is itself a leftover of the earlier team boundary.
gaps.verifyBy: read .github/CODEOWNERS for rules matching .buildkite/pipelines/boton/*.cue and .buildkite/pipelines/banking_solutions/{deploy,pre-merge}-{mintburn,stablecoinrewards}.cue

gaps.title: stablecoins-autopen CVM Terraform and its stblcn certificates sit under an HSM-owned path
gaps.detail: The CVM's own definition lives in terraform/environments/gcp/<env>/ironclave-<env>/stablecoins_autopen.tf, and its client and server certificate secrets are declared in the same directory's secrets.tf, both under a path owned by the HSM/Ironclave side rather than the stablecoins team. gaps.verifyBy: read .github/CODEOWNERS for the terraform/environments/gcp/*/ironclave-* paths, then confirm the intended split with the HSM/Ironclave and stablecoins teams

gaps.title: Stablecoins end-to-end test stack definitions are unowned
gaps.detail: The stablecoins block in nonpop-e2e-team-assets.yaml and the stablecoins_e2e_services definitions in the docker-compose and bake files have no CODEOWNERS entry, so the asset set and service list the end-to-end suites run against can change without the team noticing.

gaps.title: None of the five systems has a devstack dependencies.yaml
gaps.detail: No system in this atlas ships a dependencies.yaml and none appears in deploy/stacks, so devstack cannot bring any of them up as part of a shared stack. gaps.title: Cloud Deploy team labels are inconsistent across the stablecoins services
gaps.detail: The team label applied to the Cloud Deploy targets differs between the stablecoins services, so ownership-based filtering and reporting over deploy targets is unreliable. It is part of a broader set of stale ownership markers, alongside the stablecoinrewards deploy README template that still names Banking Solutions and its sentry-check team of banking-solutions.
gaps.verifyBy: read releases/clouddeploy_targets_v2.tf and compare the team labels on the mintburn, boton and stablecoinrewards targets

gaps.detail: The kyc_pre_merge configuration includes an autopengateway database entry, which does not match the deployed reality: the gateway's database is an Ironclave Cloud SQL instance holding the endorsement audit log, not a monorepo-provisioned service database. libraries.summary: lzconfig is the LayerZero bridging configuration library and its own Go module. It ships one embedded JSON file per environment (data/chains.{production,development,staging,local}.json) compiled into the binary, so the configuration is immutable at runtime — nothing can change a bridging pathway without a code change, review and redeploy. That makes adding or editing an entry a security change to a trust anchor: the file names the DVN signer addresses, the LayerZero protocol contracts and the adapter contracts a bridge message is verified against, so a wrong or malicious entry would redirect trust rather than merely misconfigure a client. Schema: Config{Chains, SharedDecimals=6}; each Chain carries vm (EVM or SVM), networkId, chainId, plus the LayerZero endpoint id (eid) and validator id (vid) and a dvnSignerAddress; protocolContracts holds endpointV2Address, sendUln302Address and receiveUln302Address; anchorageContracts holds Anchorage's own DVN contracts keyed by trust tier (production-token and test-token, each with an ADMIN_ROLE wallet) plus adapters and thirdPartyAdapters; each Adapter carries tokenName, assetId, oAppAddress, tokenAddress, proxyAdminAddress, feeDeposit, confirmations, localDecimals, peers, a bridgeMethod of BURN (Anchorage-minted tokens are burned on the source chain) or LOCK (third-party tokens are locked), a dvnType naming the trust tier to verify with, and walletsByRole (DEFAULT_ADMIN, FEE_CONFIG_MANAGER, RATE_LIMITER_MANAGER, PAUSER, UNPAUSER, PROXY_ADMIN_OWNER, MESSAGE_NILIFIER, MESSAGING_CHANNEL_MANAGER). Pathways per environment: production has ethereum (eid 30101 / chainId 1, DVNs for both tiers, the USDX adapter at oApp 0x36276D5c5FD8c1B900c71591708787D0034d41B5 on token 0x1014d9122960aDcf30851805ccFDde4998b4338C, peers [bsc], BURN, dvnType test-token, 18 local decimals, and third-party HADRON_USDX LOCK plus USAT LOCK on the production-token tier at 96 confirmations), bsc (30102 / 56) and celo (30125 / 42220, third-party only); development has hoodi (40449 / 560048) and bsc-testnet (40102 / 97) with a HADRON_USDX entry; staging has the same two chains but no adapters; local has anvil-src (40449 / 31337), anvil-dst (40102 / 31338) and arbitrum-regnet (90101 / 412346). The schema supports SVM as a vm value, but no SVM chain is populated in any environment (see gap-lib-lzconfig-no-svm). Consumed by mintburn and boton, both pinned at v0.5.0.

Shared Temporal declarations for the issue/redeem family of workflows: the workflow and activity names (workflows.go, activities.go), the result strings that workflows return to their parents (result_strings.go), the signal channel names the workflows wait on (channels.go), a generic RunChildWorkflow[Param, Return] wrapper that starts a child workflow and unwraps its typed result (run_child_workflow.go:15), and HandleWorkflowCancellation, which runs a caller-supplied cleanup when a workflow is cancelled and keys it by issueRedeemID (workflow_cancellation.go:14). Keeping these in a library rather than in the service means parent and child workflows agree on names and result strings at compile time. Consumed by mintburn.

The on-chain detection side of stablecoins, living inside the gethwatcher service and co-owned with the Protocols C team, so changes here need their review as well as the stablecoins team's. It holds a hardcoded list of Anchorage's mintable and burnable stablecoin addresses (knownStablecoinAddresses at line 44, with IsKnownStablecoinAddress as the lookup) and the unpackers UnpackStablecoinMint and UnpackStablecoinBurn. The important detail: mint and burn are detected from the ERC-20 Transfer event by the direction of the zero address — a Transfer with from == 0x0 is a mint and a Transfer with to == 0x0 is a burn — not from dedicated Mint or Burn events, and verifyTransferEventSignature is the only event signature the file accepts. Addresses cover regnet and testnet tokens (USDX through USDX7 on Arbitrum regnet, TODEX, USDXHoodi 0x9aEB226ab0C181040C967E94126587B416FcC6A6, USDXBscTestnet, USDTBXHoodi, aBTCHoodi, USDXMorphHoodi, GOLDXEthereumSepolia) and mainnet tokens (USDX and USDXBsc both 0x1014d9122960aDcf30851805ccFDde4998b4338C, USDXArbitrumMainnet, USDTB 0xC139190F447e929f090Edeb554D95AbB8b18aC1C, USDTBXArbitrumMainnet, FUSD and FUSDBsc both 0x1676b80EDD36B18a3C3432c11Ed25D37FdE9c92A, aBTC, USDGOMorphMainnet, TODEXEthereumMainnet, GOLDXEthereumMainnet). Consumed by the gethwatcher scanner strategies erc20_mint_detection.go and erc20_burn_detection.go. There is no Solana analogue: Solana mint/burn classification lives in autopengateway's solanaissuance decoder instead. A stray EigenLayer contracts link sits in the header comment above the address list and appears to be copy-paste residue (see gap-lib-ethcontracts-comment).
